implementation_notes: The JDK ships the container-level realization: CopyOnWriteArrayList and CopyOnWriteArraySet implement every mutative operation by copying the backing array, so traversal works on a stable snapshot and its iterator never throws ConcurrentModificationException - the right choice when reads vastly outnumber writes. For arbitrary values the refcounted handle is not idiomatic (there is no intrusive count in java.util; a hand-written AtomicInteger plus deep clone works but gives up the GC's simplicity), so the idiomatic shape is the immutable snapshot: build a new value and publish one volatile/final reference, with List.copyOf/Map.copyOf/Set.copyOf (Java 9+) or Guava's ImmutableList providing the unmodifiable snapshot and AtomicReference carrying the single-value case.
pitfalls: CopyOnWriteArrayList copies the whole array per mutation: adding in a loop is quadratic, so build a plain List and construct the collection once.
Its iterator is a snapshot: elements added after the iterator was created are never visited, and iterator remove/set/add throw UnsupportedOperationException.
List.copyOf/Map.copyOf are shallow and reject nulls; a copied list over mutable elements is only as immutable as those elements.
Memory churn grows with collection size on every write - keep copy-on-write collections small and read-mostly (listeners, handlers, configuration).
